k-1.x_notes: Six substantive problems, all on actual-size boards with block icons inline, and a clean header, footer and one-time shared rules. P1 covers shapes with blues or marks X, and it includes an even-area impossible trapezoid (8 triangles, 5 up and 3 down). P2 asks for the fewest greens in triangles of side 2-4 (2, 3, 4). P3 asks for all blue tilings of the unit hexagon (2) and the 2-1-1 hexagon (3), with spare copies. P4 asks for the fewest blocks from the full palette (3, 3, 4, verified). P5 is a strategy game: take turns placing a blue on five boards and decide whether to go first or second. The answers vary (first, second, first, first, second), and it is real math that children will replay. P6 asks for all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon, a K-1 entry to kernel 2. Weaknesses: P6 asks for drawings on half-size grids, which is fiddly for kindergartners, and 'say why' is a stretch at this age, though it is fine with the adult.
k-1.y_notes: Seven problems on actual-size boards in a large, readable font. P1 (same-color fills of a hexagon) is an easy warm-up. P2 asks for the 10 piece-combinations that fill a hexagon, with 12 actual-size copies to fill. This is good hands-on counting, though the definition 'same if they use the same pieces' is subtle. P3 counts greens in triangles (4, 9, 16, then predict 25) and is arithmetic-flavored. P4 asks for the fewest greens (2, 3, 4, predict 5). P5 is a possible/impossible set with an even-area impossible 6-triangle shape. P6 asks for the fewest pieces for a side-3 triangle (3) and a side-2 hexagon (6). P7 asks children to invent 6- and 8-triangle shapes that blues cannot fill, which is a strong creative task. The math is all correct. Weaknesses: a Name field and a non-standard header on every page, which his format forbids. P1 and P3 lean toward the 'dumbed down' side he complains about. Kernel 2 does not appear.
k-1.reason: Both are correct and keep K-1 busy on actual-size boards. X's problems are all substantive, and its first-or-second game and first look at the different tilings of a hexagon give more mathematical variety. Y opens with lighter counting tasks and puts a Name field on every page.

grades-2-3.x_notes: This is a strong kernel-1 development. P1 has a star (tileable), a side-3 triangle (odd), an even-area 7-to-5 trapezoid (impossible) and a 2-1-1 hexagon. P2 puts holes in boards: two up-holes (impossible), one up and one down (possible), and a bowtie that is balanced but impossible because the halves touch only at a point. P3 asks for the fewest greens in triangles of side 2-5, then why no one can do better. P4 asks about sides 10 and 100. P5 is a chevron-versus-blue table; the chevron answers are 4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5, a real contrast, and it asks whether chevrons can ever beat blues. P6 asks children to invent a connected 20-triangle board that needs at least 6 greens, an excellent capstone. P7 asks for a rule for two green holes on the side-2 hexagon. I verified that every up/down pair works, so the 'one up, one down' rule is exactly right, and there are 10 small hexagons for recording tries. All boards are actual size, with recording lines. Minor weaknesses: 'explain' is appended to most problems, and the P1/P2 wording repeats.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Nearly the same arc, and also correct. P1 has five boards: a star, two even-area imbalanced trapezoids, a balanced board with a unique tiling that makes a real puzzle (verified), and an odd 15-triangle board. P2 has hole boards: up+down is possible, down+down is not. P3 asks for the two-hole rule on the side-2 hexagon. P4 has board J, balanced 7-7 but impossible because two down triangles compete for one up triangle. P5 uses large boards for triangles of side 3-6, P6 asks about sides 10 and 100 with 'how do you know nobody can use fewer', P7 asks about chevron packings, and P8 compares the purple and blue boards. The questions are open, and less 'explain' is appended. Weaknesses: a Name field and a non-standard header on every page. There is no recording space for the rule problem and no writing space anywhere. The rule problem comes before the triangle work that consolidates the counting idea. The final purple-versus-blue question is fairly easy.
grades-2-3.reason: The mathematics and sequence are almost the same and both are sound. X ends with stronger tasks (inventing a board that needs at least 6 greens, and the rule problem with places to record tries), and it follows his page format. Y's unique-tiling board and board J are nice, but Y has Name fields and less workspace.

grades-4-5.x_notes: This is a well-developed kernel 2 that follows the outline closely. P1 asks for all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon and how you know. P2 builds the flip graph, but children must redraw all 6 tilings, which duplicates P1. P3 asks children to build three specified pairs on an actual-size side-2 hexagon and find the fewest flips. I decoded the pictures and the answers are 3, 4 and 8, contrasting and correct, and E to F is the diameter. P4 asks for a 4-flip round trip that never flips the same hexagon twice in a row, then whether 5 or 7 flips is possible. P5 defines ribbons with a correct LRRLR example and L/R icons, and asks what one flip does to the ribbons. P6 asks for proofs of even round trips and the 8-flip lower bound. P7 asks children to count all 20 tilings, with 25 copies. P8 asks for the tilings of the 1-3-3 hexagon (20). It is concrete and hands-on, with flips done physically. Weaknesses: a full page of lines for proof writing, frequent 'explain' prompts, the redraw in P2, and no cube-stack connection.
grades-4-5.y_notes: A good kernel-2 packet, and all of it is correct. P1 asks for the 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon on 8 copies. P2 maps the flips with dots and lines, which is more efficient than redrawing. P3 defines ribbons with a correct RLRR example, then asks which strings occur and whether two coverings can share a ribbon, an elegant open route to the bijection. P4 counts the 1-2-3 hexagon (10) and the 1-4-4 hexagon (70), which forces a counting idea. P5 asks for all 20 tilings of the side-2 hexagon. P6 is one flip pair, X to Y (4, verified). P7 asks for the pair that is the most flips apart (8). P8 asks whether a round trip can take an odd number of flips. P9 shows a covering drawn as stacked cubes, asks what a flip does to the stack, and asks for the full box (8). Weaknesses: the Name field and header. There is only one concrete flip-distance example. Flips are never tied to ribbons, and the cube tool comes after the parity question it would help with. Problems and boards are split across pages.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are mathematically rich and correct. Y adds the cube picture and the elegant 70-tiling generalization. X gives more concrete flip work (three contrasting pairs on a physical board, the constrained round trip) and connects flips to ribbons, which is the outline's central argument.

overall.reason: The two packets are close in mathematical quality and every problem I checked in both is correct. X is slightly better in each band: the K-1 game and first look at different tilings, the 2-3 invention capstone and recording space, and the concrete 4-5 flip work tied to ribbons. X also follows his page format, while Y puts a Name field and a non-standard header on every page that he would need to edit out. Together these make X the clear choice.
